q1511: Article 7 covers the citizenship rights of people who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947: they are not citizens of India unless they came back under a resettlement permit.
Article 6: migrants from Pakistan to India. Article 8: persons of Indian origin living abroad.
q1512: The Kendriya Hindi Sansthan (Central Institute of Hindi) has its headquarters in Agra, Uttar Pradesh.
It trains teachers of Hindi as a second or foreign language.
q1513: Trachoma is an eye infection caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis; repeated infection can cause blindness. WHO declared India free of trachoma as a public-health problem in 2024.
It spreads through flies and contact with eye discharge.
q1514: Uday Shankar, the pioneer of modern Indian dance, mixed classical, folk and Western stagecraft in his dance dramas; he set up the Almora cultural centre (1938).
He was the elder brother of sitar maestro Ravi Shankar.
q1515: Portable art from India's Upper Palaeolithic includes ostrich eggshell beads and engraved eggshell fragments, as found at Patne (Maharashtra).
Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh) has the famous prehistoric rock paintings.
q1516: Qutbuddin Aibak died at Lahore in 1210 after falling from his horse while playing chaugan (polo).
He is buried at Anarkali Bazaar, Lahore.
q1518: Under the National Clean Air Programme (launched 2019), the revised target is a cut of up to 40% in PM10 levels by 2025-26 from the 2017-18 baseline, in 131 non-attainment cities.
q1519: The incorrect statement is that chlorine is the most electronegative element. Fluorine is. The others hold: halogens are group 17, highly reactive non-metals, and occur as gas (F₂, Cl₂), liquid (Br₂) and solid (I₂).
Chlorine has the highest electron affinity; fluorine the highest electronegativity.
q1520: Sugarcane needs a hot, humid climate (21–27°C) and 75–100 cm of rain; Uttar Pradesh is the largest producer.
Wheat, gram and mustard are cool-season rabi crops.
q1521: Yamini Krishnamurthy, the Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi exponent, received the Padma Shri (1968), Padma Bhushan (2001) and Padma Vibhushan (2016).
She ran a dance institute in Delhi.
q1522: National income equals total factor payments, which in turn equals the value of all final goods and services produced — the gross domestic product.
The circular flow: output = income = expenditure.
q1525: The National Commission for Scheduled Castes (Article 338) has a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson and three other members, appointed by the President.
The separate National Commission for STs (Article 338A) came with the 89th Amendment (2003).
The National Commission for Scheduled Castes has 1 Chairperson, ______ Vice-Chairperson and ______ members.
q1526: Operation Flood (1970, NDDB, led by Dr Verghese Kurien) was the White Revolution in dairying, a form of animal husbandry, which made India the world's largest milk producer.
National Milk Day is 26 November, Kurien's birthday.
Which non-farm employment is associated with Operation Flood?
q1527: In the Joint Liability Group model, 4–10 borrowers guarantee each other's loans. The group pressure cuts credit risk and raises repayment rates without collateral.
NABARD has promoted JLGs for tenant farmers since 2006.
In microfinance in India, what is the significance of the 'Joint Liability Group (JLG)' model?
It ensures compliance with environmental sustainability standards.
It provides government subsidies to support agricultural investment.
It enables group-based lending to reduce credit risk and increase repayment rates.
It allows MFIs to diversify their loan portfolios across sectors.
q1528: In NCERT's Köppen classification of India, Arunachal Pradesh has the Dfc type: a cold, humid winter with a short summer.
Amw (monsoon with short dry season): the west coast south of Goa. BWhw (hot desert): western Rajasthan.
According to the Köppen classification, which type of climate is found in Arunachal Pradesh?
Amw – monsoon with short dry season
Dfc – cold humid winter with short summer
q1529: W. C. Bonnerjee presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress in Bombay in December 1885.
A. O. Hume was the founder-general secretary.
Who presided over the Indian National Congress session held at Bombay in 1885?
q1530: Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to offspring through genes.
Genetics is the study of heredity and variation; Mendel is its father.
The biological process by which traits pass from one generation to the next is called __________.
q1531: After the Mauryan decline, regional kingdoms rose in parts of Ashoka's former empire: the Satavahanas in the Deccan and Kharavela's Mahameghavahana dynasty in Kalinga.
Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription is at Udayagiri, near Bhubaneswar.
Which regions were part of Ashoka's empire where kingdoms emerged after the decline of Mauryan rule?
q1534: A mansabdar was an officer holding a mansab (rank) in Akbar's system, which fixed his status, pay and the cavalry he kept.
Zat = personal rank; sawar = cavalry number.
In the Mughal empire, whom did the term 'mansabdar' refer to?
A person holding a position or rank
q1535: A Governor resigns by writing to the President of India (Article 156).
The President also appoints the Governor.
The Governor of a state addresses his resignation to __________.
The Chief Minister of the state
q1536: Article 345 lets a state legislature adopt one or more languages as official languages of the state; Uttarakhand used it in 2010 to make Sanskrit its second official language.
Himachal Pradesh also made Sanskrit a second official language (2019).
Under Article ______ of the Constitution, the Uttarakhand Assembly passed a proposal in 2010 making Hindi the official language and Sanskrit the second official language of the state.
q1537: Henry's law: the partial pressure of a gas in the vapour phase is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution (p = K_H·x) — gas solubility rises with pressure.
That is why soft drinks are bottled under high CO₂ pressure.
Which law states that the partial pressure of a gas in the vapour phase is proportional to the mole fraction of the gas in the solution?
q1538: The Indian bison (gaur) has been listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 1986 because its population is falling.
The gaur is the largest wild cattle species.
Since 1986, in which IUCN category has the Indian bison been listed because of its declining population?
q1539: The Hindi novel 'Pataliputra ki Samragyi' is by Sharad Pagare.
His novel 'Pehla Satyagrahi' is about Kalinga's Kharavela.
The famous book 'Pataliputra ki Samragyi' is associated with ________.
q1541: The Lorenz curve shows the degree of income inequality: the further it bows below the line of equality, the more unequal the society.
The Gini coefficient is calculated from the Lorenz curve.
In income distribution, what does the Lorenz curve measure?
The degree of income inequality in a society
The total income generated in a country's economy
The concentration of wealth among the richest individuals
The share of income earned by different quintiles of the population
q1542: Mohiniyattam, named after Mohini (Vishnu's enchantress form), is the classical dance of Kerala.
The dance form named after the mythical character Mohini belongs to which state?
q1544: Money works as a medium of exchange, a unit of account (not a 'unit of labour'), a store of value and a standard of deferred payment.
Barter fails without a 'double coincidence of wants', which money solves.
q1545: Agar is a jelly-like substance obtained from red algae such as Gelidium and Gracilaria, used in labs and food.
Carrageenan also comes from red algae; algin from brown algae.
q1546: Palms belong to the Arecaceae family of monocot flowering plants.
The coconut and the date palm are also Arecaceae.
Palm trees belong to which plant family?
Arecaceae, a family of monocot flowering plants
Fabaceae, a family of leguminous flowering plants
Moraceae, a family of tropical flowering plants
Pinaceae, a family of coniferous evergreen plants
q1548: Jelep La and Nathu La, in Sikkim, lie on the old Indo-Tibet trade route through the Chumbi Valley.
Nathu La reopened for India–China border trade in 2006.
q1549: 'The Argumentative Indian' (2005) is by Amartya Sen, who celebrates India's tradition of public debate.
Also by Sen: 'Development as Freedom', 'The Idea of Justice'.
q1550: Bihar has the highest share of multidimensionally poor people in NITI Aayog's Multidimensional Poverty Index; Kerala has the lowest.
The MPI uses three dimensions: health, education and standard of living.
q1551: Sri Thyagaraja Government College of Music and Dance was set up in Hyderabad in 1952 to promote Indian music and dance.
It is named after the Carnatic composer Tyagaraja.
q1552: Census 2011: Kerala had the highest sex ratio among states, 1,084 females per 1,000 males.
q1553: In March 1940 Udham Singh shot Sir Michael O'Dwyer in London, avenging the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919), when O'Dwyer was Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab.
Udham Singh was hanged in July 1940 at Pentonville Prison.
In 1940 Udham Singh killed a British officer in London. Who was the officer and why was he targeted?
Lord Zetland – Secretary of State for India, targeted for supporting colonial repression
Jack Gibson – a British officer unconnected with the Jallianwala Bagh massacre
Michael O'Dwyer – to avenge his role in the Jallianwala Bagh massacre
Charles Innes – a former Viceroy of India, targeted for unrelated colonial policies
q1554: Only transverse waves can be polarised, so polarisation proves that light is a transverse wave.
Sound in air is longitudinal and cannot be polarised.
q1555: ISRO was formed on 15 August 1969, replacing INCOSPAR; its headquarters is in Bengaluru.
India's first satellite, Aryabhata, was launched in 1975 on a Soviet rocket.
q1556: Bori (Pune district) and Morgaon are Lower Palaeolithic sites in Maharashtra; Bori is among the oldest in India.
Other Lower Palaeolithic sites: Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu), Hunsgi (Karnataka), Bhimbetka.
q1557: The Administrator of Dadra and Nagar Haveli also served as Administrator of Daman and Diu; since 26 January 2020 the two are merged into one UT.
q1560: Part IVA (Article 51A) deals with Fundamental Duties, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).
Fundamental Duties are not enforceable in court.
q1561: Someshvara I (1042–68) of the Western (Kalyani) Chalukyas moved the capital from Manyakheta to Kalyani (Basavakalyan, Karnataka).
Vikramaditya VI started the Chalukya–Vikrama era; Bilhana wrote his biography.
q1563: The Kendriya Hindi Sansthan was set up in 1961 under the Ministry of Education (then HRD), with its headquarters at Agra.
The Central Hindi Directorate was set up in 1960.
q1564: Baul is the mystic folk music of Bengal (West Bengal and Bangladesh), sung by wandering minstrels with the ektara. UNESCO lists it as intangible heritage.
Bhavageete is from Karnataka; Bihugeet from Assam.
q1565: Kud is a folk dance of Jammu and Kashmir, performed at night to honour Lok Devtas. Bagh Nach and Ghumura (Odisha) and Chhau (Odisha, Jharkhand, Bengal) are from eastern India.
Chhau has three styles: Seraikela, Purulia and Mayurbhanj.
q1566: Babur lost his ancestral kingdom of Fergana and Samarkand to the Uzbeks under Shaibani Khan, another Central Asian (Mongol-descended) group. He then took Kabul and later invaded India.
Babur descended from Timur on his father's side and Genghis Khan on his mother's.
q1567: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal on 16 October 1905, observed as a day of mourning; the Swadeshi movement followed.
Tagore started Raksha Bandhan as a symbol of unity against the partition.
q1568: Kati (Kongali) Bihu in October–November is when Assamese farmers light earthen lamps in the paddy fields to pray for the standing crop.
The three Bihus: Rongali/Bohag (April, new year), Kati/Kongali (October), Bhogali/Magh (January, harvest).
q1569: Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of the laws.
It applies to citizens and non-citizens alike.
q1570: India's sex ratio in 1901 was 972 females per 1,000 males; it fell for most of the 20th century to 927 in 1991.
q1571: Harappans practised bronze casting widely, using the lost-wax technique; the Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro is the best-known example. They did not use iron.
Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.
q1572: Bandhan Financial Services and Bandhan Bank are headquartered in Kolkata; Bandhan started as a microfinance NGO in 2001 and became a universal bank in 2015.
IDFC First Bank also got a universal bank licence in 2014-15.
q1573: The 17th Lok Sabha election (2019) recorded the highest voter turnout of any general election, about 67.4%.
q1574: Vijayanagara's four dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu. 'Yaduha' was not one.
q1575: Article 80 fixes the Rajya Sabha's maximum strength at 250 (238 elected + 12 nominated).
Article 81 sets the composition of the Lok Sabha.
q1576: Bakho-Bakhain and Panwariya are folk dances of Bihar.
Other Bihar dances: Jat-Jatin, Jhijhiya, Bidesia (folk theatre).
q1577: The Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761) was fought between the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau and Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani) with his allies; the Marathas were defeated.
Ahmad Shah Durrani founded modern Afghanistan.
q1578: The amalaka is the ribbed stone disc on top of the shikhara of Nagara (north Indian) temples, with a kalasha above it.
Garbhagriha: sanctum. Antarala: vestibule. Jagati: raised platform.
q1579: A Vernier caliper measures internal and external dimensions (and depth) accurately, to about 0.1 mm.
A screw gauge (micrometer) is more precise, to about 0.01 mm.
q1580: The President could nominate two Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha (Article 331) until January 2020; the 104th Amendment (2019) ended this.
The same amendment extended SC/ST reservation by 10 years, to 2030.
q1581: Swami Vivekananda was born Narendranath Datta in Calcutta on 12 January 1863, now observed as National Youth Day.
He spoke at the Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago, in 1893.
q1582: Article 5 dealt with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950), based on domicile together with birth or residence.
q1583: The Ministry of Culture lists 9 classical dances, adding Chhau to the Sangeet Natak Akademi's 8: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam and Sattriya.
Sattriya (Assam) was the last added by the Akademi, in 2000.
Many books still say 8 (the Sangeet Natak Akademi list). This question's key follows the Ministry of Culture, which gives 9.
q1584: Krishnadevaraya (1509–29) of the Tuluva dynasty was Vijayanagara's most celebrated king.
The Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes described his capital, Hampi.
q1585: Bastar Dussehra in Jagdalpur, Chhattisgarh, runs for about 75 days and honours goddess Danteshwari, not Rama.
It is among the longest festivals in the world.
q1586: The 69th Amendment (1991) added Articles 239AA and 239AB, making Delhi the National Capital Territory with an elected Legislative Assembly.
The Balakrishnan Committee recommended the change.
q1587: The Sawai Gandharva Bhimsen Mahotsav, a major Hindustani classical music festival, is held in Pune every December; Pandit Bhimsen Joshi started it in 1953.
Bhimsen Joshi (Kirana gharana) received the Bharat Ratna in 2009.
q1588: The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes was created in 2004 when the 89th Amendment (2003) split the old Article 338 commission, adding Article 338A for STs.
Article 338 now covers the National Commission for SCs.
Strictly, the NCST sits in Article 338A, inserted by amending Article 338.
q1589: N. K. Singh chaired the Fifteenth Finance Commission (2021-26 award period).
The Sixteenth Finance Commission (2026-31) is chaired by Arvind Panagariya.
q1590: A chaitya is a Buddhist prayer hall (place of worship) with a stupa at its far end; a vihara is a monastery where monks live.
Karla and Bhaja (Maharashtra) have famous rock-cut chaityas.
q1591: The Lalit Kala Akademi (National Academy of Art) was inaugurated in New Delhi in 1954.
Sangeet Natak Akademi and Sahitya Akademi were also set up in the early 1950s.
q1592: Census 2011: Haryana had the lowest sex ratio among states, 879.
Its child sex ratio (834) was also the lowest.
q1593: Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (25 December 2000) gives all-weather road links to unconnected rural habitations as part of poverty reduction.
It is run by the Ministry of Rural Development.
q1594: India and Nepal signed the Kosi Agreement in the mid-1950s for the Kosi barrage and embankments; the barrage stands at Bhimnagar on the Nepal side.
The Kosi is called the 'Sorrow of Bihar'.
The Kosi Agreement is usually dated 25 April 1954; Nepal is correct either way.
q1595: The Supreme Court upheld 27% OBC reservation from the Mandal Commission report in Indra Sawhney (November 1992); the key takes 1992 as the year it came into effect after the verdict.
The same verdict set the 50% ceiling and excluded the 'creamy layer'.
The V. P. Singh government's order came in 1990 and the post-verdict order in September 1993; DSSSB's key marks 1992, the verdict year.
q1596: The Right to Information Act, 2005 came fully into force on 12 October 2005.
It set up the Central and State Information Commissions.
q1597: Wind is a non-traditional (non-conventional, renewable) energy source. Petroleum, coal and natural gas are conventional fossil fuels.
Tamil Nadu and Gujarat lead India in wind power.
q1598: Article 30 gives religious and linguistic minorities the right to establish and run educational institutions of their choice.
Article 29 protects any section of citizens' distinct language, script or culture.
q1599: Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in January 2016.
Sikkim won the UN FAO's Future Policy Gold Award in 2018.
q1600: 'Bani Thani', called 'India's Mona Lisa', belongs to the Kishangarh school of Rajasthani painting and was painted by Nihal Chand in the 18th century.
A 1973 Indian postage stamp showed Bani Thani.
q1601: The nucleus is the dense, usually round body at the centre of a cell that controls its activities and holds the DNA.
Robert Brown discovered the nucleus in 1831.
q1602: Limestone is a non-metallic mineral, mainly calcium carbonate, used for cement. Copper, silver and gold are metallic.
Other non-metallic minerals: mica, gypsum, salt.
q1603: Iodine deficiency causes goitre (swelling of the thyroid), since iodine is needed to make thyroxine.
India's iodised salt programme fights iodine deficiency.
q1604: Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment; 16(4) allows reservation for backward classes.
q1605: A magnet always has two poles (north and south); a magnetic monopole has never been found. Cut a magnet in half and each piece has both poles.
Magnets attract iron, point north–south when free, and like poles repel.
q1606: Pure (neutral) water has a pH of 7 at 25°C.
Below 7 is acidic (lemon juice ~2); above 7 is basic (soap ~10).
q1607: The Economic Survey was first presented in 1950-51 as part of the Union Budget and was separated from the Budget documents in 1964.
It is prepared by the Chief Economic Adviser and presented a day before the Budget.
q1608: Wildlife sanctuaries, national parks and biosphere reserves protect flora and fauna. An amusement park is for entertainment.
India's first national park: Hailey (now Jim Corbett), 1936.
q1609: Himachal Pradesh's Manikaran (Parbati valley) has hot springs where India's geothermal energy potential was explored with a pilot plant.
Puga valley in Ladakh is India's most promising geothermal site.
q1610: Credit unions are member-owned financial cooperatives whose members share a common bond, such as the same profession (teachers) or organisation (military).
In India, cooperative credit societies play a similar role.
q1611: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water; land is about 29%.
Oceans hold about 97% of Earth's water; freshwater is about 3%.
q1612: After the Pokhran-II tests in May 1998, Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee declared India a nuclear weapon state.
The tests were code-named Operation Shakti; 11 May is National Technology Day.
q1613: The first phase of the Civil Disobedience Movement was called off after the Gandhi–Irwin Pact in March 1931.
It resumed in 1932 and was formally withdrawn in 1934.
Some books take 1934, when the movement was finally withdrawn; DSSSB's key marks 1931.
q1614: The Northern Plains were formed by three river systems and their tributaries: the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra.
They are divided into the Punjab plains, Ganga plains and Brahmaputra plains.
q1615: Meteoroids are small rocky pieces moving around the Sun; one burning in Earth's atmosphere is a meteor (shooting star), and one reaching the ground is a meteorite.
Asteroids are larger rocky bodies, mostly between Mars and Jupiter.
q1616: The Malwa Plateau is the lava upland north of the Vindhyas, with the Aravallis to its north-west; it is drained by the Chambal and Betwa.
The Bundelkhand and Baghelkhand uplands lie to its east.
q1617: Chapchar Kut, Mizoram's spring festival, is held in March after jungle-clearing for jhum (shifting) cultivation.
Other Mizo festivals: Mim Kut and Pawl Kut (harvest).
q1618: In the Battle of Poona (October 1802) Yashwantrao Holkar defeated Peshwa Baji Rao II and Daulat Rao Scindia; the Peshwa fled and signed the Treaty of Bassein (1802) with the British.
This led to the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05).
q1619: Census 2011: India's population density was 382 persons per sq km.
q1620: Moonlight is sunlight reflected off the Moon, so it is reflection, not refraction. A bent pencil in water, a rainbow and a coin appearing raised are all refraction.
A rainbow uses refraction, dispersion and internal reflection.
q1621: Karuna means compassion or pathos, not humour (humour is hasya). The other pairs are right: shringara–love, adbhuta–wonder, bibhatsa–disgust.
The nine rasas: shringara, hasya, karuna, raudra, veera, bhayanaka, bibhatsa, adbhuta, shanta.
q1622: The main coffee plant is Coffea arabica (Arabica); Coffea canephora (Robusta) is the other major species.
India mostly grows Arabica and Robusta in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
q1623: The Slave dynasty (1206–90) is also called the Mamluk dynasty, since Qutbuddin Aibak and several successors had been slaves ('mamluk').
It is also called the Ilbari dynasty.
q1624: Article 51A, which lists the Fundamental Duties, is in Part IVA of the Constitution.
Part IVA has only this one Article.
